title: Three Roman rules for discerning Divine and Apostolic traditions — first rule
source_text: XVI. Porro Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae plures tradunt regulas, quibus traditiones revera divinae & Apostolicae discerni possint ab aliis, quae falso possent pro talibus obtrudi. Quae tamen omnes regulae ad tres reduci possunt. Prima est quod quicquid Ecclesia Romana tanquam de fide credit, nec tamen in Scriptura clare traditum reperitur, hoc ipso censendum est traditionem esse divinam, seu Apostolicam. Idque nititur duobus quae supponunt fundamentis. Unum est quod Ecclesia Romana errare non possit: Alterum quod tamen Ecclesia illa hodie non regitur novis revelationibus: sed quicquid novit in rebus fidei id totum ab Apostolis & Prophetis didicit.
pass_a_gloss: Moreover the doctors of the Roman Church hand down several rules by which traditions that are truly divine and Apostolic may be discerned from others that could falsely be thrust forward as such. Yet all those rules can be reduced to three. The first is that whatever the Roman Church believes as of the faith, and yet is not found clearly handed down in Scripture, is by that very fact to be counted a divine or Apostolic tradition. And that rests on two foundations which they suppose: one, that the Roman Church cannot err; the other, that nevertheless that Church is not today governed by new revelations, but whatever it knows in matters of faith it learned entirely from the Apostles and Prophets.
pass_b_english: Roman doctors offer several tests for sorting true Divine and Apostolic traditions from fakes; they boil down to three.

First: whatever Rome believes as de fide, yet is not clearly in Scripture, must itself be a Divine or Apostolic tradition — because Rome cannot err, and because she is not ruled by fresh revelation but only by what she learned from Apostles and Prophets.
